finding: The $170 floor of the live range looks about right for one front caliper. The $825 top covers everything we could build, but all three independent benchmarks reach above it, so the top may be somewhat low for dealer quotes and for cars with costly calipers. Built totals for one front caliper, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks), with no fluid bleed charge, pads or core charge: economy 2015 Toyota Corolla about $152-$441 ($79.95 house-brand caliper with bracket to $280.92 Toyota list, 0.6-1.0 hr); midsize 2015 Hyundai Sonata about $206-$496 (0.8-1.0 hr); truck/SUV 2016 Dodge Durango about $166-$337 (0.6-1.0 hr); luxury 2017 Cadillac XT5 about $212-$331 (1.0 hr), plus a $40 core charge if the old caliper is not returned. The bottom: our lowest totals are about $152 and $166 (an $80-$94 aftermarket caliper with bracket and a 0.6-hour warranty time), so $170 is a fair floor; a real quote will usually be higher because it adds brake fluid and bleeding. The top: the dearest caliper we priced for the basic Sonata gives about $496, and the larger-brake Sonata calipers on the same Hyundai catalog page list at $516-$563, which with 1.0 hr comes to about $680-$725, so $825 leaves some room for a bleed. Against that, the benchmarks run higher. Jerry gives $300-$1,500 for a single caliper, on one to three hours of labor and genuine European calipers at $685-$821 each. YourMechanic's mobile quotes for one caliper on a Honda Civic are $453-$627, with shop/dealer prices of $504-$987 for the same jobs. RepairPal's national average is $898-$968 on about $749 in parts, several times the list price of any single caliper we found, and its page does not say whether that is one caliper or an axle. (ConsumerAffairs' $500-$1,500 for a single caliper is RepairPal's data restated, not a separate check.) The gap between our totals and these figures is mostly things outside this unit: bleeding and fluid, new pads, shop parts markup over online prices, longer billed times than warranty times, and vehicles we did not price. We did not price a European luxury car or a multi-piston performance caliper, which Jerry's examples show can cost four to five times the calipers here. So the range is about right for the bare job on mainstream vehicles, and the top is a lead to recheck with a European example, not a settled result. How solid the labor times are: all are manufacturer warranty times from recall bulletins, which is good, but warranty times are the low end of what shops bill (Jerry's general figure is one to three hours). Midsize (0.8 hr), truck/SUV (0.6 hr) and luxury (1.0 hr) are for the example vehicle itself; economy is a Mazda3 time (0.6 hr), not a Corolla. The upper end of 1.0 hr for economy, midsize and truck is the GM time for a different vehicle. Because half of the eight hour figures are not for the example vehicle, the confidence stays low even though every class now has a stated time and at least two parts sources. Only one bulletin (2015 Chevrolet Colorado, both front calipers, 1.2 hr) says the time includes bleeding the brakes; the others do not say. What is still missing: an aftermarket or remanufactured price for the XT5 (its low end is a discounted genuine part; none was found on the pages that loaded), a Corolla-specific labor time, and a stated time for a half-ton pickup. A re-check on 2026-11-20 looked at moving the economy example to the 2020 Mazda3, since the Mazda recall time (0.6 hr one side, 0.7 hr both; the document does not mention bleeding) is for that car. The genuine Mazda front left caliper BCYA-33-99ZB (padless, 2019-2025 Mazda3) lists at $374.21 on one Mazda parts catalog and $368.68 on another, but no aftermarket or remanufactured front caliper for the 2019-on Mazda3 was found on any retailer page that loaded (the ones found fit 2014-2018 only), so the example was not changed and the Corolla figures stand. No new stated time for one front caliper on a Corolla, a Sonata, a Durango or a half-ton pickup turned up either. The Corolla low end is a retailer house-brand caliper taken from the retailer's fitment list (2009-2018 Corolla); its 2015 listing page could not be loaded.
extras: A quote usually adds brake fluid and bleeding the brakes (often charged as a brake fluid service). Many shops replace calipers in pairs on the same axle, which roughly doubles the parts and adds less than double the labor (manufacturer bulletins allow 0.7-1.4 hr for both fronts against 0.6-1.0 hr for one). Also common: new brake pads on that axle (a leaking or seized caliper often ruins them; the bulletins add 0.1-0.2 hr), rotors if they are scored or overheated, a new brake hose, a caliper bracket and hardware when the caliper is sold without them, a core charge that is refunded when the old caliper is returned (remanufactured and some genuine calipers; $40 on the Cadillac part), a brake inspection or diagnosis fee, shop supplies and sales tax. Rear calipers with a built-in parking brake, electric parking brakes and multi-piston performance calipers cost more.
